bc_lower_red_tail.blurb: Lower Red Tail is a face-climbing sector at Skaha Bluffs, above Penticton in the Okanagan, and the first piece of the Red Tail Group you meet on the walk up from the lot. Nearly all of its 26 lines are bolted, with a couple of top-rope and trad options mixed in. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.10 in an even spread, so it works well for newer leaders and for warming up. The climbing is edgy and technical on gneiss. Spring and early fall are the busiest seasons at Skaha.
bc_lower_red_tail.parking_note: Leave the car in the main climbers' lot at the end of Smythe Road and continue on foot; avoid blocking the narrow road on busy days.
bc_lower_red_tail.approach: From the lot, head up the hill past The Fortress. Lower Red Tail is the first part of the Red Tail Group on the way. A second way in leaves the slope before or after Another Buttress.

bc_cascade_gorge.blurb: Cascade Gorge is a compact roadside crag in the Boundary country, close to Grand Forks and Christina Lake, where the river cuts through the rock. Its 26 routes are short, roughly 8 to 12 metres, and mostly bolted, with a few trad lines. The grades lean toward 5.10 and 5.11, with a scattering of easier climbs from 5.3 up through 5.9. Some of the climbing is steep and juggy, and a few lines are thin and technical. Many routes sit right beside the water, which makes it a pleasant place to cool off on a hot day. Some top anchors and longer lines call for slings or extended draws.

bc_the_monastery.blurb: The Monastery is one of the hard sport crags in Cheakamus Canyon, in the Chek area north of Squamish along the Sea to Sky corridor. All 26 routes are bolted, and nearly all are 5.11 and up: the bulk sit at 5.12 and 5.13, with a few 5.14s and a lone moderate. The wall is mildly overhanging and changes character from left to right, from a short steep overhang to a continuous prow, a vertical section that stays fairly dry in rain, and a mixed right side with slabby faces. It faces east, catching the morning sun and falling into shade in the afternoon.

bc_foreplay_left.blurb: Foreplay Left is the main wall of Foreplay Cliff, one of the Evergreen Drive crags at the north end of Skaha Bluffs near Penticton. It holds 25 routes, almost all bolted, with a single trad line. The wall is slightly overhanging and faces west, staying cool into early afternoon before taking the late sun, which makes it a good choice when the rest of the valley is baking. Grades are firmly in the middle and upper range: a handful of 5.10s, then mostly 5.11 and 5.12, plus one 5.13 and one easy outlier. Not the place for beginners.

bc_old_unsorted_routes.blurb: Old Unsorted Routes is a mixed bag of about 25 climbs in the Stillwater area, a seaside spot roughly 20 minutes south of Powell River on the Sunshine Coast. Short trad routes make up about half, backed by top-rope lines, a handful of boulder problems and a single aid route. Roped grades range from the 5.4 range up to the low 5.12s, though most fall between 5.7 and 5.10, and the boulder problems run from VB to a hard V6. Cliffs here rise from the shoreline, with boulders in the forest behind, and the rock dries quickly after rain. A relaxed, low-key place to wander between climbs.

bc_greenwood_park.blurb: Greenwood Park is a small, quick-hit bouldering spot in North Vancouver, close to Lynn Valley and the highway, reached from the north end of Moody Avenue. The boulders and small walls sit in shaded woods in what was once a quarry, and the landings are mostly flat. Its 25 problems are friendly: V0 is the biggest group, then a steady thinning through V1 to V4. Expect slabs, cracks, sloper holds, jug starts and a few traverses. It suits a couple of hours of easy bouldering after work, and is a good place for newer boulderers.

bc_funarama.blurb: Funarama is a small trad-focused crag tucked into the Smoke Bluffs, the climbing park right beside Squamish, near the trail that links the Elephant's Arse and Octopus Garden zones. It is split into an upper and lower section. Of its 25 routes, nearly all are trad, with one bolted line. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.11, and about ten sit at 5.10. Expect finger cracks and rolling, less-than-vertical slabs on granite, some of them technical tests of footwork. The wall faces south, so it warms quickly in summer and is best on cooler days or early in the morning.
